questions.question:
Consider the following logical inferences. I1: If it rains then the cricket match will not be played.
The cricket match was played.
Inference: There was no rain.
I2: If it rains then the cricket match will not be played.
It did not rain.
Inference: The cricket match was played.

Which of the following is TRUE?

options.A: Both I1 and I2 are correct inferences
options.B: I1 is correct but I2 is not a correct inference
options.C: I1 is not correct but I2 is a correct inference
options.D: Both I1 and I2 are not correct inferences

questions.explanation:
Let R = it rains, M = match is played. Rule: [latex]R\rightarrow\neg M[/latex].

- I1: M is true, so [latex]\neg M[/latex] is false [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] R must be false (modus tollens) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] valid.
- I2: [latex]\neg R[/latex] does not tell us anything about M (denying the antecedent) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] invalid.

Answer: I1 is correct but I2 is not a correct inference

questions.question:
In a room there are only two types of people, namely Type 1 and Type 2. Type 1 people always tell the truth and Type 2 people always lie. You give a fair coin to a person in that room, without knowing which type he is from and tell him to toss it and hide the result from you till you ask for it. Upon asking, the person replies the following

"The result of the toss is head if and only if I am telling the truth."

Which of the following options is correct?

options.C: If the person is of Type 2, then the result is tail
options.D: If the person is of Type 1, then the result is tail

questions.explanation:
Let H = "result is head".

- Type 1 (truthful): the statement is true and he is telling the truth, so H [latex]\leftrightarrow[/latex] True gives H.
- Type 2 (liar): the statement is false and he is not telling the truth. "H [latex]\leftrightarrow[/latex] False" is false only when H is true.

Either way the result is head.

Answer: The result is head

questions.question: Two people, P and Q, decide to independently roll two identical dice, each with 6 faces, numbered 1 to 6. The person with the lower number wins. In case of a tie, they roll the dice repeatedly until there is no tie. Define a trial as a throw of the dice by P and Q. Assume that all 6 numbers on each dice are equi-probable and that all trials are independent. The probability (rounded to 3 decimal places) that one of them wins on the third trial is
questions.explanation:
A trial ties with probability [latex]\frac{6}{36}=\frac16[/latex]. Someone wins on the 3rd trial if the first two tie and the third does not:
[latex]\left(\frac16\right)^2\times\frac56=\frac{5}{216}\approx0.023[/latex]

Answer: 0.023

questions.question:
[latex]g(. )[/latex] is a function from [latex]A[/latex] to [latex]B[/latex], [latex]f(. )[/latex] is a function from [latex]B[/latex] to [latex]C[/latex], and their composition defined as [latex]f(g(. ))[/latex] is a mapping from [latex]A[/latex] to [latex]C[/latex].
If [latex]f(. )[/latex] and [latex]f(g(. ))[/latex] are onto (surjective) functions, which ONE of the following is TRUE about the function [latex]g(. )[/latex]?

options.C: [latex]g(. )[/latex] must be a bijective function, that is, both one-to-one and onto.
options.D: [latex]g(. )[/latex] is not required to be a one-to-one or onto function.

questions.explanation:
We're told [latex]f[/latex] is onto (B→C) and the composite [latex]f\circ g[/latex] is onto (A→C), and asked what this forces about [latex]g[/latex] (A→B).

Intuitively: since [latex]f[/latex] alone is already onto [latex]C[/latex], every element of [latex]C[/latex] has some preimage in [latex]B[/latex] regardless of [latex]g[/latex]. The fact that [latex]f\circ g[/latex] is also onto just says [latex]g[/latex]'s image happens to hit enough of [latex]B[/latex] to cover all of [latex]f[/latex]'s "useful" preimages — but [latex]g[/latex] itself doesn't need to be onto all of [latex]B[/latex] (there could be elements of [latex]B[/latex] entirely outside [latex]g[/latex]'s range, as long as [latex]f[/latex] still reaches every element of [latex]C[/latex] through the range [latex]g[/latex] does cover), nor does [latex]g[/latex] need to be one-to-one (multiple elements of [latex]A[/latex] could map to the same element of [latex]B[/latex]).

A simple counterexample confirms it: let [latex]B=\{1,2\}[/latex], [latex]C=\{1\}[/latex], [latex]f[/latex] onto, and [latex]g[/latex] mapping every element of [latex]A[/latex] to just [latex]1\in B[/latex] — [latex]g[/latex] is neither onto nor one-to-one, yet [latex]f\circ g[/latex] is trivially onto.

Answer: g(.) is not required to be a one-to-one or onto function.

questions.question: Let [latex] A  [/latex] be the adjacency matrix of a simple undirected graph [latex]G[/latex]. Suppose [latex]A[/latex] is its own inverse. Which one of the following statements is always TRUE?
questions.explanation:
[latex]A=A^{-1}\Rightarrow A^2=I[/latex].

- [latex](A^2)_{ii}[/latex] = degree of vertex [latex]i[/latex] = 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] every vertex has exactly one neighbour.
- [latex](A^2)_{ij}=0[/latex] for [latex]i\ne j[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] consistent with that.

A graph where every vertex has degree exactly 1 is a set of disjoint edges covering all vertices [latex]\text{---}[/latex] a perfect matching.

Answer: G is a perfect matching

questions.question:
A function [latex]f:\mathbb{N}^{+}\rightarrow \mathbb{N}^{+}[/latex], defined on the set of positive integers [latex]\mathbb{N}^{+}[/latex], satisfies the following properties:
f(n)=f(n/2) if n is even
f(n)=f(n+5) if n is odd
Let R={[latex]i|\exists j:f(j)=i[/latex]} be the set of distinct values that f takes. The maximum possible size of R is ____.
questions.explanation:
Both rules keep a number inside its class:
- If n is a multiple of 5, n/2 (when even) and n + 5 are still multiples of 5.
- If n is not a multiple of 5, neither are n/2 and n + 5.

Within each class all values are linked (e.g. 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 6 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 8 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 4 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 1, and 5 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 10 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 5), so f can take at most one value per class: at most 2 values.

Answer: 2

questions.question:
In a directed acyclic graph with a source vertex s, the quality-score of a directed path is defined to be the product of the weights of the edges on the path. Further, for a vertex v other than s, the quality-score of v is defined to be the maximum among the quality-scores of all the paths from s to v. The quality-score of s is assumed to be 1.

The sum of the quality-scores of all vertices on the graph shown above is ______
questions.explanation:
Go in topological order, taking the best product into each vertex:
- s = 1, c = 1, a = 9
- f = c [latex]\times[/latex] 9 = 9, b = a [latex]\times[/latex] 1 = 9
- d = max(c [latex]\times[/latex] 1, a [latex]\times[/latex] 1) = 9
- g = max(f [latex]\times[/latex] 1, d [latex]\times[/latex] 9) = 81
- e = max(d [latex]\times[/latex] 9, b [latex]\times[/latex] 1) = 81
- t = max(g [latex]\times[/latex] 1, e [latex]\times[/latex] 9) = 729

Sum = 1 + 1 + 9 + 9 + 9 + 9 + 81 + 81 + 729 = 929

Answer: 929

questions.question:
There are two elements x,y in a group (G,*) such that every element in the group can be written as a product of some number of x's and y's in some order. It is known that
x * x = y * y = x * y *x * y = y* x * y *x = e
where e is the identity element. The maximum number of elements in such a group is _______.
questions.explanation:
[latex]x^2=y^2=e[/latex] and [latex](xy)^2=e[/latex] give [latex]xy=(xy)^{-1}=y^{-1}x^{-1}=yx[/latex], so x and y commute.

Every product then reduces to one of e, x, y, xy (the Klein four-group).

Answer: 4

questions.question:
Which one of the following options is CORRECT given three positive integers x, y and z, and a predicate
[latex]P(x)=\neg (x=1)\wedge \forall y(\exists z(x=y*z))\Rightarrow (y=x)\vee (y=1)[/latex]

options.A: P(x) being true means that x is a prime number
options.B: P(x) being true means that x is a number other than 1
options.C: P(x) is always true irrespective of the value of x
options.D: P(x) being true means that x has exactly two factors other than 1 and x

questions.explanation:
P(x): x [latex]\ne[/latex] 1, and whenever y divides x (x = y[latex]\cdot[/latex]z), y must be 1 or x.

So x has no divisors other than 1 and itself, i.e. x is prime.

Answer: P(x) being true means that x is a prime number
